title: NASA crash-tests aircraft under a gantry built for Moon-landing practice

cover.alt: A silver, egg-shaped test aircraft body lies on packed earth after being dropped, in front of a tall white wall marked with a grid.

body: NASA Langley's **Lunar Landing Research Facility**, finished in 1965 for $3.5 million, was a giant A-frame gantry with an overhead crane. A full-size lunar module simulator hung from it so astronauts could practise the last 150 feet (46 m) of a landing on the Moon. After Apollo, the same steel frame was put to work dropping aircraft: renamed in 1974, it hosted crash research until 2003, then reopened in 2005 to test the Orion capsule. Engineers still hoist test aircraft up and let them fall, to see how well their structures protect the people inside.

slides.alt: A full-scale air-taxi body swings in on cables and slams into the ground in front of a gridded wall, then a camera inside shows crash dummies jolted in their seats.
slides.caption: NASA Langley, June 2025: a full-scale air-taxi body, released from the gantry, swings in and hits the ground. Inside, crash-test dummies take the jolt.
slides.credit: NASA Langley Research Center · Public domain · excerpt

slides.label: astronauts practised Moon landings at the gantry
slides.text: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin among them. They flew a mock lunar module, powered by a small rocket motor, over a simulated lunar landscape.

slides.heading: One steel frame, many jobs
slides.note: A splashdown pool for capsule tests was added beneath the gantry in 2011

slides.heading: Why drop an air taxi?
slides.text: In the [2025 test](https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/armstrong/nasa-drop-test-supports-safer-air-taxi-design-and-certification/), the body was hoisted about 35 feet (11 m) and dropped with a 10-degree twist, a US safety-certification condition. Its crushable floor, like a car's crumple zone, seemed to work.

slides.question: Which part of a Moon landing did Apollo astronauts rehearse at the gantry?
slides.explanation: The crane-hung simulator let them practise solving the piloting problems of the final 150 feet (46 m) down to the surface.
